title: EU-wide comparison of the characteristics and presentation of branded food products (2021)
abstract_text: Differences in composition of seemingly identical branded food products (DC-SIP) occur when a good is marketed in one Member State as being identical (same brand labelling and same or similar front-of-pack appearance) to a good marketed in another Member State while that good has a significantly different composition or significantly different characteristics. The Joint Research Centre (JRC) developed a common testing methodology to examine the occurrence of this practice in the European single market. This methodology was applied in the first EU-wide testing campaign in 2018/2019. The objective of this study is to replicate the 2018/2019 testing campaign to provide figures for 2021 on the occurrence of DC-SIP in the European single market and to compare them with the results of the 2018/2019 testing campaign. In addition to the result of this comparison, this report presents the results of a survey of brand owners about their (potential) actions regarding DC-SIP in response to recent regulatory changes, namely the amended Directive 2005/29/EC – the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) – where a specific provision on DC-SIP (Article 6(2)(c)) was introduced by Directive (EU) 2019/2161.

title: Neighborhood disadvantage, frailty, and cognitive performance approaching midlife in the Colorado Adoption/Twin Study of Lifespan behavioral development and cognitive aging (CATSLife)
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Frailty is associated with poorer cognitive functioning and both have been associated with neighborhood deprivation. Whether such associations are apparent before midlife may provide a perspective on whether and how neighborhoods serve as a risk or resilience factor. The present study tested whether the association between neighborhood deprivation and cognitive functioning is mediated by frailty. METHODS: We analyzed data from 1163 CATSLife participants (Mage = 33 years, range 28-49; 53% female, 10% non-white/Hispanic; tested between 2015-2021) with available age 16 IQ assessments. A general cognitive ability (GCA) factor was extracted from nine specific cognitive ability tests assessed by CATSLife and t-score scaled. A 30-item frailty index (FI), previously associated with processing speed, was included. A 2010 Area Deprivation Index (ADI) measure was constructed from seven census features (i.e., income, high school education, owner-occupied units, poverty, unemployment, contract rent, female-headed households) using a decile approach and averaged. FI and ADI were z-scored before analysis. In path analysis, we regressed GCA on FI, and both were regressed on ADI, adjusting for adolescent IQ, age, sex, race/ethnicity, adoption status, and sibling similarity. We replicated findings with unranked 2018 Social Vulnerability Index SES scores (SVI-SES) and WAIS-III IQ scores. RESULTS: Higher 2010 ADI was associated with higher FI (B=0.139, p <0.001) and lower GCA (B=-0.426, p = 0.042), and higher FI was associated with lower GCA performance (B = -0.588, p = .011). The indirect effect between 2010 ADI and GCA via FI was significant (Indirect Estimate = -0.082, p = 0.031). Similar patterns were observed with the 2018 SVI-SES, for FI and GCA (Indirect Estimate=-0.126, p = 0.026), FI and full-scale IQ (Indirect Estimate=-0.098, p = 0.069), and FI and performance IQ (Indirect Estimate=-0.160, p = 0.033), albeit not always achieving statistical significance. CONCLUSION: Adjusting for adolescent IQ, we observed associations of neighborhood disadvantage with lower general cognitive ability performance at midlife that may be connected via shared associations with frailty. Future work will expand to health behaviors (e.g., brain care scores) and further test temporality and selection factors.

title: Historical Atmospheric Lead Concentrations (1960‐1974) and Memory Problems Half a Century Later: Findings from Two Large, Independent Representative Samples
abstract_text: Abstract Background Lead exposure has adverse impacts on cognition and dementia risk factors such as hypertension. A major historical source of lead exposure was via atmospheric pollution due to leaded gasoline. Method We mapped historical atmospheric lead levels (HALL) in the contiguous US using measurements obtained by the US EPA from 1960 to 1974, a period of high leaded gasoline combustion. We extrapolated HALL by kriging and calculated mean HALL for each public use microdata area (PUMA). Our analyses include only PUMAs which contained at least one lead measurement in 1960‐74. We obtained individual‐level data of self‐reported memory problems, from the American Community Survey (ACS) in two time periods, 2012‐2017 ( n = 368,208) and 2018‐2021 ( n = 276,476). The samples were restricted to respondents aged 65 and older living in their natal state. We calculated odds ratios using HALL as the exposure variable and self‐reported memory problems as the outcome, controlling for respondents’ age, sex, race/ethnicity, and education. We used individuals in PUMAs with the lowest HALL (< 0.4 µg/m 3 ) as reference in comparison to those in PUMAs with moderate (0.4‐.79 µg/m 3 ), high (0.8‐1.19 µg/m 3 ) and extremely high HALL (>=1.2 µg/m 3 ). Result In the 2012‐2017 ACS, in comparison to older adults living in PUMAs with the lowest HALL, the odds of reported memory impairment were higher in those in PUMAs with moderate (Odds ratio (OR)=1.21; 95% CI=1.17‐1.25), high (OR=1.21; 95% CI=1.17‐1.25) and extremely high HALL levels (OR=1.19; 95% CI=1.13‐1.25). We replicated the study using 2018‐2021 ACS data and found comparable outcomes for older adults living in PUMAs with moderate (OR = 1.17; 95% CI=1.12‐1.21), high (OR=1.20; 95% CI=1.16‐1.25) and very high HALL (OR=1.22; 95% CI=1.15‐1.29). Conclusion We observed in two very large ( n >250,000) independent representative samples that older adults had approximately 20% higher odds of reporting memory problems if they lived in PUMAs that had HALL > 0.4 µg/m 3 compared to <0.4 µg/m 3 . This adds to the evidence implicating lasting health outcomes, including cognition, due to earlier life lead exposure from air pollution. The precipitous decline in atmospheric lead exposure in the last quarter of the 20 th century may help to explain the declining incidence of dementia in the US.

title: Impressions of a dating profile that communicates conspiracy theories - Study 2
abstract_text: The current study builds on Study 1 (osf.io/ptsfm). In Study 1, participants exposed to a dating profile that expressed a conspiracy theory (i.e., "Covid-19 is a hoax, people") reported the person in the profile as being less honest, less trustworthy, less sociable, less intelligent, less kind, less friendly, less respected, and more unique, compared to a dating profile which expressed an anti-conspiracy message (i.e., "Covid-19 is real, people") and a control condition which did not express any conspiracy theory. Further, participants also showed lower intentions to meet or to get into a relationship with the person in the pro-conspiracy dating profile, compared to the anti-conspiracy profile and control. No differences in impressions and intentions to meet were found between control and anti-conspiracy condition. In the current study, we will conceptually replicate these findings by presenting a different conspiracy theory in the pro- and anti-conspiracy conditions: "The 2020 election was rigged" versus "The 2020 election was not rigged". We also include a new impression variable: quirkiness. Like need for uniqueness, we expect participants to rate the pro-conspiracy profile (vs. control and anti-conspiracy conditions) as being more quirky. We also explore a new impression variable: potential relationship satisfaction. In Study 1, we also examined participants' own conspiracy belief as a moderator of these effects. We found that the negative effects of the pro-conspiracy condition (compared to the anti-conspiracy condition) on intentions to meet (friendly and intimately), impressions of friendlessness, kindness, trustworthiness, and honesty were more pronounced in participants who were low in conspiracy beliefs. In the current study we aim to replicate these effects. We will also explore need for uniqueness and interpersonal trust as potential moderators.

title: From pollution halo to haven: Two-sided environmental spillovers of foreign firms in China
abstract_text: This study replicates and extends the analysis of Kim et al. (Journal of International Business Studies, 53(7): 1370–1393, 2022). Kim et al. (2022) provide evidence that the presence of foreign firms improves the environmental performance of nearby domestic firms, using data on industrial enterprises in Jiangsu, China from 2000 to 2007. This study examines whether this relationship holds over a longer period and across a broader geographic scope. We first replicate their analysis using the original data source, then extend it to a nationwide panel of industrial firms from 2000 to 2013. We find that the proximity of foreign firms improves local firms' environmental performance when foreign firm activity, measured by sales or numbers, is relatively low. However, beyond a certain threshold, some foreign firms appear to loosen environmental standards to gain competitive advantage, prompting imitation by local firms and leading to higher emissions. We also show that community-based and industry-based institutional channels significantly moderate these spillover effects. These findings contribute to the literature on the environmental impact of foreign direct investment and deepen understanding of the mechanisms underlying the environmental spillover effects of multinational enterprises.

title: The impact of violence at home to psychoemotional distress, well-being and suicidal risk: a massive mental health screening using smartphones
abstract_text: Violence at home and mental health disorders are psychosocial factors related to suicidality. In Mexico, these factors are claimed to be associated with suicides from adolescents to elders. This study aimed to replicate a study undertaken in 2019 to explore the relationship between well-being and suicidality, adding violence at home together with emotional distress in the Mexican State of Yucatan after the COVID-19 outbreak. A cross-sectional study was carried out with 32,530 citizens who were surveyed using a smartphone app, and partial least squares structural equation models were applied. We examined whether domestic violence operates primarily indirectly—via depression or anxiety—on suicidality and whether associations differ by gender. A total of 17,846 complete cases (from 15 to 80 years old) responded. Depression showed the strongest direct association with suicidality, with concomitant links to higher anxiety and lower well‑being. Domestic violence had no direct path to suicidality but showed a significant total (indirect) effect via depression and anxiety. Gender‑stratified models indicated differences across sex; namely, a non‑significant anxiety to suicidality path among women, and a non‑significant well‑being to suicidality path among men. Domestic violence was reported as frequent/very frequent a 12.0% of the sample, high suicidality in 10.3%, clinically relevant anxiety in 12.2%, and low well‑being in 27.3%. Well-being was protective against suicidal risk except in men, while anxiety was unrelated to suicidality in women. Findings support a stress–appraisal pathway where domestic violence acts as a chronic stressor primarily increasing suicidality indirectly via emotional distress, with gender-specific patterns. At system level, population-scale digital screening can complement community detection and referral in Yucatán.

title: Aggregation and Organic Matter Protection Following Tillage of a Previously Uncultivated Soil
abstract_text: Understanding the effects of tillage on soils following years or decades of no-till is critical for developing C conservation strategies. To date, short-term responses to tillage in previously uncultivated or other long-term no-till soils have primarily focused on total C changes, which are difficult to detect. Tillage effects on soil conservation and C permanence may be better predicted by changes in more readily detected factors known to affect C storage such as aggregation and physically protected C. We annually plowed replicated plots in a previously uncultivated midsuccessional field between 2002 and 2004 and investigated changes in the distribution of aggregates, physically protected C, and light fraction (LF) organic matter. Within 60 d of initial cultivation, soil aggregates in the 2000- to 8000-μm size class declined from 0.47 to 0.15 g g−1 at 0- to 7-cm soil depth and from 0.32 to 0.23 g g−1 at 7 to 20 cm. Lower levels of aggregation persisted through the winter and spring of the following year. Inter-aggregate, unprotected light fraction (LF) increased following cultivation, as did particulate C in soil fractions with densities < 1.9 g cm−3 Changes in the mass of total soil C were not detectable after 3 yr but the vertical distribution of all soil C pools was altered by plowing. Our study demonstrates that plowing once immediately and substantially alters aggregation and LF and particulate C dynamics and that these conditions persist. Results suggest that no-till soils need to be continuously maintained to protect aggregation and physically stabilized C pools.

title: University of Michigan Transportation Security Index Survey Data and Project Reports (2022 and 2024)
abstract_text: <p>&nbsp;</p> <p>This project, titled &ldquo;Developing a 3-itemTransportation Security Index,&rdquo; developed and validated a 3-item Transportation Security Index (TSI), a measure designed to directly capture the experience of transportation insecurity at the individual level regardless of mode of transit or geography. Planners, researchers, and policy makers needed an even shorter form than the existing validated 16-item long form (TSI-16) and 6-item short form (TSI-6). To that end, we used nationally representative survey data collected in 2022 to first identify a 3-item short form (TSI-3). We then replicated and validated this short form by fielding an original nationally representative survey in 2024. To validate the short form, we used the 2024 data to assess the level of agreement between the TSI-3 and the TSI-6. We also compared the predictive power of each of these TSI forms by examining how they were associated with key outcomes, including physical and mental health.&nbsp;</p> <p>&nbsp;</p> <p>The study was determined to be exempt by UM IRB (protocol number HUM00096242)</p>

title: Sediments of the Hackensack River
abstract_text: The sediments of the Lower Hackensack River provide a record of contamination from ongoing and historical processes in a highly urbanized watershed in northern New Jersey. This estuarine river runs through suburban and small cities in its northern, freshwater reaches; passing south through 8,500 acres of wetlands known as the Hackensack Meadowlands to its mouth at Newark Bay. The goal of this review is to depict the environmental quality of this ecosystem using data derived from sediments collected in 2003 during a Fishery Resource Inventory. This study replicated a similar inventory conducted in 1988, allowing for elucidation of spatial and fifteen-year trends. In the sediments, heavy metal concentrations, grain size distribution and carbon content were analyzed. Based on sediment guidelines published by NOAA in 1995, the estuary is in “poor” ecological condition; the average concentration of one contaminant, mercury, exceeds the ERM (ERM is the median concentration of a contaminant observed to have adverse biological effects in the literature values examined). It is also apparent that enrichment of mercury and other metals occurs in the Hackensack River north of the mouth of Berry’s Creek, a major tributary known for its legacy of industrial contamination. In addition to this spatial trend, a good predictor of metal concentrations in the sediments appears to be the amount of organic matter present; preservation of organic matter in the river increases as tidal influence is diminished. The sulfate/sulfide cycle, driven by the reaction between seawater and the organic matter, appears to be the primary mechanism. Between 1988 and 2003, the average sediment concentrations were reduced significantly for cadmium (71%), chromium (63%), copper (73%) and lead (22%); zinc concentrations remained approximately the same (mercury was not analyzed in 1988). These results suggest a natural attenuation process at work, as burial preserves sulfide rich contaminated sediments.

title: Teaching Social Work Policy Classes in a Divisive Era: Student Suggestions to Promote Civil Classroom Dialogue
abstract_text: Social work instructors are navigating educational environments that are impacted by the divisiveness apparent within society today, but few resources exist to guide them. This article attempts to contribute practical guidance for educators, especially those teaching about political issues where students, and perhaps even instructors, may possess differing perspectives that juxtapose with the official mandates of social work. This study replicated a prior study that examined the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election results by employing the same method with an updated survey to examine the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election. First, this article begins with a literature review examining current scholarship addressing this issue and potential frameworks to inform instructors, which involve adapting a critical teaching pedagogy and grounding course content in social work ethics and values. Next, through a mixedmethod approach, MSW students completed a survey related to the 2024 U.S. Presidential election, including questions on political divide in their classrooms and ideas for instructors to promote civil discussions. The data were compared with the previous study and revealed insightful shifts in student political division and participation, and offered recommendations for instructors to promote inclusivity in the classroom.

title: Affect Labeling and Reappraisal as an Emotion Regulation Strategy
abstract_text: Affect labeling, the process of identifying and verbally expressing emotions, is being increasingly studied as a naturally occurring emotional process with regulatory consequences. Despite the growing interest, the mechanisms underlying affect labeling remain unclear, with studies yielding contradictory results. While some research supports its positive impact on emotional regulation, a study by Nook et al. ( 2021 ) found that affect labeling hindered subsequent reappraisal, highlighting the need for further investigation. This study replicates and extends Nook et al. ( 2021 ), hypothesizing that the positive effects of affect labeling on reappraisal might emerge over time. In two studies (total N = 226), participants were randomly assigned to four conditions, varying in their use of affect labeling and reappraisal while viewing 24 negatively valenced images. Participants either passively observed, labeled affect, reappraised, or combined labeling and reappraisal. Participants rated their emotional responses immediately and again one to two days later. Results of both studies mirrored those of Nook et al. ( 2021 ), with affect labeling reducing the effectiveness of reappraisal. However, follow-up measurements did not support the hypothesis of delayed positive effects, instead showing a return to baseline measures. These findings suggest that the effects of affect labeling and reappraisal diminish over time. The study corroborates Nook et al. ( 2021 ), indicating that affect labeling may solidify emerging emotions and limit emotional regulation flexibility.

title: Study 2 - Cross-temporal SEM Replication
abstract_text: This study is a cross-temporal replication and extension of a previously conducted survey (2024) examining how perceived AI threat and loss of control shape public attitudes toward AI through institutional trust (government trust and corporate trust) and conspiracy beliefs, based on Van Prooijen's Existential Threat Model. The original study employed structural equation modeling (SEM) with a Chinese adult sample (N = 2,008) and established a mediation pathway from existential concerns and institutional distrust to conspiracy-driven resistance toward AI. The present study replicates this survey with a new sample of Chinese adults (target N = 2,000–3,000) in 2026, a period marked by rapid AI advancement and increased public exposure to AI technologies. The primary goals are to (1) test the measurement invariance of the original scales across the two time points, (2) examine whether the original SEM pathways can be replicated, and (3) compare key variable means across the two time points. If replication fails, we will explore whether observed changes in path coefficients reflect psychological adaptation to AI proliferation.

title: Does a hard-to-read font reduce the causality bias? Registered replication exploring individual differences
abstract_text:

78-15: We will exclude participants based on the result of the ANOVA using the degree that participants are currently studying as the grouping variable. If this analysis reveals significantly lower causal judgments for any of the critical groups (i.e. psychology, gender studies, ai engineering) we would assume that they are not naive to the contingency learning task and that including their results would compromise the main analyses. Therefore, if one group shows significantly lower judgments, we will exclude their data.

Based on previous studies (Díaz-Lago and Matute, 2019; Dalla-Bona and Vicovaro, 2023) and assuming some absenteeism of the scheduled participants, we will not stop collecting data until we reach a minimum of 60 participants per group. This means that every participant will see, in a randomized order:

-15 "c" trials (cue absent and outcome present)

78-21: Does a hard-to-read font reduce the causality bias? Registered replication exploring individual differences

78-23: Experiment

78-7: Following our 2019 study (https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500004848) in which results showed a debiasing effect of the illusion of causality under disfluent conditions (i.e., contingency learning task information presented in a hard-to-read font), Dalla-Bona and Vicovaro ran a replication that yielded non-significant results (https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218231220928 , Exp.2).
Trying to address possible differences between studies (e.g. university students vs. Prolific sample; in-person vs. online procedure), we conducted an unpublished study in which we partially replicated the original finding when accounting for individual differences. Concretely, intelligence (measured with the short version of Raven's progressive matrices) correlated negatively with the illusion of causality only when the information was presented in a hard-to-read font, suggesting that the debiasing effect could take place under difficult conditions that triggers deliberative (System 2) processes depending on the cognitive resources of the individual. Furthermore, when excluding participants due to suspected technical problems (all of outlier participants in the hard-to-read group in the easiness of reading question to check the font manipulation were the only ones in that running the experiment using the Firefox browser in that group, stating a contradictory "easiness in reading" when, allegedly, the presented font was Mistral), we also replicated the original main effect.
Considering this theoretical and empirical background, we aim to directly replicate our original finding in a sample similar to the 2019 study (i.e. university students), while including intelligence (short version of Raven's progressive matrices) and meta-cognitive measures (Spanish version of the Metacognition Self-Assessment Scale) since we suspect that these variables could variables that potentially would explain the differences between university students and Prolific sample.
Therefore, the main question is: 
(1) Does a hard-to-read font reduce the causality bias in a university student sample? The main hypothesis to be tested is
H1: Causal judgments in a null-contingency causal learning task are expected to be lower for participants that perform the experiment in a hard-to-read font compared to an easy-to-read font control group

We would also address the following exploratory questions:
(2) Does intelligence play a role in debiasing when disfluency acts as a metacognitive cue of difficulty?
H2: Raven's progressive matrices scores are expected to negatively correlate with causal judgments only for participants that performed the task in a hard-to-read font
(3) Does metacognition play a role in the debiasing effect of disfluent conditions?
H3: Metacognitive Self-Assessment Scale (MSAS) scores are expected to negatively correlate with causal judgments only for participants that performed the task in a hard-to-read font

To check consistency of H1 and the robustness of the effect of the letter type on causal judgments, we will address the following question:
(4) Can we predict the illusion of causality based on the perceived easiness of reading?
H4: Scores in the easiness of reading question are expected to positively correlate with causal judgments

78-9: The main dependent variable to test H1 is the Causal Judgment. It is a unique response in a 0-100 scale of a question that participants have to answer after seeing 40 fictitious patients that could have taken (or not) a drug (cue) that is non-contingent to a possible (or not) recovery. The exact wording of the question, in Spanish, is the following "¿Hasta qué punto crees que el Batatrim ha sido efectivo para curar las crisis de los pacientes que has visto?", where 0 indicates no causal relationship between the two events. The individual participant's response would be stored in a variable named Causal Judgment.

The variable to explore H2 is the total score in the short version of Raven's progressive matrices. It is a scale that could range from 0-9, 0 indicating no hits in the test. There are 9 progressive matrices to solve. The answers for each will be aggregated into one total score per participant to form the Raven total score variable.

The variables to explore H3 are the total score of the MSAS and the score of the 4 factors of the scale. There are 18 statements to which participants could answer in a scale from 1-5, where 1 is "Never" and 5 is "Almost always": 7 statements corresponds to the Self-Reflectivity factor, 3 to the Critical Distance, 3 to the Understanding Others Minds, and 5 to the Mastery factor. The answers would be aggregated to calculate each factor and the total score for the MSAS in variables named as Self-Reflectivity, Critical Distance, Others Minds, Mastery, and total MSAS.

The variables to test H4 are the perceived easiness of reading, measured using a single question addressing experiment's easiness of reading. Participants could answer in a 1-7 Likert scale where 1 is "Extremely hard" and 7 is "Extremely easy", and the Causal Judgment mentioned above.

We will also record:
-Age
-Gender
-Time spent in each part of the experiment (instructions, trials, judgment, MSAS, and Raven matrices)
-Four 7-point Likert scales to answer questions to check the experimental manipulation (easiness of reading, perceived quickness, perceived reading fluency, and willingness to participate again)
-Their scores in the test to access university studies
-The 40 trial sequence that they saw (a=drug and recovery present, b=drug present and no recovery, c=no drug and recovery, d=no drug and no recovery)
-Their 40 predictive responses to the question "¿Crees que el paciente superará la crisis?" asked in each trial (0=No, 1=Sí)
-The degree that participants are currently studying

-To test H1 we will conduct a one-tailed t-test for independent samples between the easy-to-read and the hard-to-read group (where easy-to-read > hard-to-read) with Causal Judgment as the Dependent Variable and Font as the grouping variable. A p-value of less than 0.05 will indicate a significant effect of Font in Causal Judgments. Effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals will be reported.  

-To test H2 we will split the dataset between the easy-to-read group and the hard-to-read group based on the Font variable to conduct separate Pearson's correlation on Raven total score and Causal Judgment
-To test H3 we will split the dataset between the easy-to-read group and the hard-to-read group based on the Font variable to conduct separate Pearson's correlations for Causal Judgment and the different MSAS scores (4 factors and total score)

-To test H4 we will conduct a Pearson's correlation for Causal Judgment and easiness of reading scores.

We will run the following analyses for manipulation checks:

title: Testing Alliance Theory in U.S. Policy Attitudes: A Replication and Extension Using ANES 2024
abstract_text:
OSF registration template: OSF Preregistration

This study uses nationally representative data from the 2024 American National Election Study (ANES) to replicate and extend a key test of the Alliance Theory of political ideology. Alliance Theory proposes that policy attitudes reflect people’s allegiance to the beneficiaries or opponents of a given policy, rather than abstract moral values like egalitarianism. We reanalyze and expand the approach used in Chapter 4 of David Pinsof’s dissertation (2018), using the updated ANES 2024 dataset. We examine policy preferences across a range of issues and test whether attitudes toward relevant social groups (e.g., Blacks, rural Americans, Christians, transgender people) better predict support for policies than general values of egalitarianism.

q2: 1. Across diverse policy domains, attitudes toward social groups associated with the beneficiaries or opponents of a given policy will significantly predict support for that policy.
2. These group-based predictors will account for unique variance in policy attitudes above and beyond general ideological values of egalitarianism.

q3: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.

q4: No blinding is involved in this study.

q6.question: This is a cross-sectional, individual-level analysis using survey data from the 2024 ANES Time Series Study. For each policy outcome, we will conduct OLS regressions including (a) egalitarianism, political party, liberal/conservative identity and (b) alliance-relevant group attitudes (e.g., feeling thermometers, perceived discrimination, group stereotypes). We replicate the logic and structure of David Pinsof’s original models but apply them to the updated 2024 ANES dataset and extend them to additional domains (e.g., transgender rights, Israel/Palestine).

q8: Registration prior to accessing the data

q9: We are using the April 30, 2025 preliminary release of the ANES 2024 Time Series Study. This includes combined pre- and post-election data. The dataset is nationally representative and includes both in-person and web-based samples, as well as a panel component.

q10.question: The ANES used a mixed-mode national sample including in-person, web, video, and phone interviews. Respondents were drawn from four independently selected sample components: (1) fresh in-person sample, (2) fresh web sample, (3) longitudinal panel from 2016/2020 ANES, and (4) GSS-linked respondents (not included in this release). Eligibility was limited to U.S. citizens aged 18+ residing in the 50 states or Washington, D.C.

q11: We will use all post-election respondents with non-missing data on outcome and predictor variables. We anticipate sample sizes of 4,000–6,000, depending on item-specific missingness.

q17.question: For each policy outcome, we will run ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions in two sequences:

Sequence 1:
	•	Step 1: Enter policy-relevant group attitude predictors (party/ideology thermometers and policy-specific group predictors as defined above).
	•	Step 2: Add the egalitarianism composite to the model.

Sequence 2:
	•	Step 1: Enter the egalitarianism composite.
	•	Step 2: Add the group attitude predictors (party/ideology thermometers and policy-specific group predictors).

All predictors will be z-scored prior to analysis.

For each sequence, we will report:
	•	Unstandardized regression coefficients (b)
	•	Standard errors (SE)
	•	p-values (3 decimal places)
	•	95% confidence intervals
	•	R² and adjusted R² for each model step
	•	Change in R² after adding the second set of predictors (group attitudes in Sequence 2; egalitarianism in Sequence 1)

This approach will allow us to examine the unique variance explained by group attitudes vs. egalitarianism and to test whether controlling for group attitudes substantially reduces the effect of egalitarianism, and vice versa, as predicted by the Alliance Theory.

q18: All continuous variables will be standardized using z-scores. Symbolic racism and egalitarianism will be averaged composites. Items overlapping conceptually with policy outcomes will be removed on a per-model basis.

q19: We will use two-tailed tests with α = 0.05. We will emphasize both statistical and theoretical significance.

q20: We will use listwise deletion within each model. Respondents missing outcome or key predictor variables will be excluded from that model.

q23: We will use the ANES post-election full-sample weight (V240107b) and apply Taylor Series variance estimation using PSU (V240107c) and strata (V240107d) variables.

title: Attending to form and meaning in processing second language input : a study of advanced second language learners
abstract_text: This study replicates VanPatten's research (1990) in order to determine whether learners of Spanish as a second language (L2) can simultaneously attend to meaning and form when processing input. My research furthers VanPatten's work through an investigation of more advanced students of Spanish L2. The participants for this study were 60 advanced Spanish L2 students at McGill University in Montreal, Canada. To investigate whether advanced L2 learners can focus on form while listening for meaning, participants were randomly assigned to complete one of four listening tasks: Task I (control task): listening to the passage for content only, Task II: listening to the passage for content and simultaneously noting the key lexical item, inflacion, Task III: listening to the passage for content and simultaneously noting the article la, and Task IV: listening for content and simultaneously noting the verb morpheme -n. Comprehension of the passage was assessed by a written recall protocol. Results revealed that comprehension scores were higher among learners listening only for meaning than those of learners attending to meaning and one of the formal features. The findings of the present study are in agreement with VanPatten (1990). Learners' attention to form while listening for meaning appears to affect comprehension.

title: Lowered Abundance of Gut Bacteriophage Species Is Associated With Human Cancer Cachexia
abstract_text: BACKGROUND: Cancer cachexia exemplifies a high medical need condition without effective treatment. Recent studies implicated bacterial gut microbiome alterations to cancer cachexia. Whether the gut bacteriophage profile, an important microbiome component for health and disease, is also related to cancer cachexia remains unknown. We aimed to profile gut microbiome alterations in human cancer cachexia with attention on bacteriophages. METHODS: We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing in stool samples from 78 cachectic and 42 noncachectic patients (53% male, mean age 67 ± 8 years) with newly diagnosed, advanced-stage (UICC IV) gastrointestinal cancers. Cachexia was defined according to the main criterion agreed upon international consensus (weight loss [WL] adjusted to body mass index [BMI]). Obtained DNA short-reads were used for k-mers-based, phage-inclusive matching with reference databases, de novo phage assembly and inferring microbiome-encoded functions. We replicated significance-based statistical and prediction-oriented machine-learning analyses in 2022 and 2025 generated metagenome datasets to incorporate the recent change by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) from morphology-based (valid until 2022) to revised genome-based phage taxonomy into microbiome findings of cachexia. RESULTS: Cachectic and noncachectic patients differed significantly regarding BMI (mean 20.9 vs. 26.4 kg/m2), WL (mean -6.5 vs. -0.2 kg), survival (median 5 vs. 13 months) and clinical cachexia domains (e.g., C-reactive proteine and appetite loss) (all p < 0.001) but not for other clinical covariables (e.g., cancer type) (all p > 0.05). Read-based mapping (2022/2025) identified 1.312/1.513 species (74/39 phage species), and de novo assembly resulted in 4.184/4.209 contigs (corresponding to 65/39 phage species). Concordantly, both analyses (2022 and 2025) showed that prevalent cachexia associated significantly with beta-diversity (Bray-Curtis distance, PERMANOVA, p < 0.05), but not to alpha-diversity (Shannon-Index, ANOVA, p > 0.05), reduced microbiome-encoded detoxification functions (e.g., enriched microbial β-glucuronidase and depleted bacterial efflux pumps) and lowered abundance of bacterial species with false-discovery-rate (FDR)-corrected p < 0.05 (2022: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Roseburia intestinalis, Streptococcus species and Lachnospiraceae species; 2025: Faecalibacterium species, Ruminococcus gauvreauii and Intestinibacter bartlettii). Further, lowered abundance of bacteriophages associated with cachexia, predominantly affecting double-stranded (2022: Caudovirales, Siphoviridae, FDR-corrected p < 0.05; 2025: Myoviridae, Siphoridae, p < 0.05) but also single-stranded (2022: Inoviridae, Microviridae, p < 0.05; 2025: Inoviridae; p < 0.05) DNA phage species. In machine-learning models, bacteriophages were top-ranked cachexia predictors (2022: Caudovirales, Siphoviridae; 2025: Myoviridae, Siphoridae). Accuracy was highest when only phage contigs were taken into account (correctly classified instances: 75.0%-85.8%; AUC: 0.703-0.916). CONCLUSIONS: The previously unknown link between gut bacteriophages and human cancer cachexia expands the scope for basic, translational and clinical microbiome-targeted research in an area of significant unmet medical need. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Study Box of the German Cancer Society (Registration Number ST-U069, Date: 29 May 2018).

title: Validating sociodemographic disparities in HPV vaccine uptake in a universal, publicly funded, low barrier, school-based immunisation program in the Vancouver Coastal Health region of British Columbia, Canada: A cross-sectional study
abstract_text: OBJECTIVES: Exploratory analysis conducted with the 2021/2022 age-eligible school cohorts identified lower vaccine coverage among grade 6 and 9 students of the Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) region who were residing in neighbourhoods facing material and social deprivation. Other determinants of lower coverage included male sex, attendance in non-faith-based independent school category, and residence in rural areas. This study aimed to replicate the analysis in the 2022/2023 cohort to assess reliability across school years less affected by the pandemic and prioritise the determinants in order to implement programmatic actions to improve HPV vaccine uptake. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of grade 6 and 9 students residing in the VCH region and attending VCH schools. A cross-classified multilevel model was developed to replicate and validate findings from the 2021/2022 cohort, describing associations between sociodemographic explanatory variables and underimmunisation. Public health priorities were informed by population attributable fractions (PAFs) from the final model. RESULTS: The final model confirmed significant associations between immunisation coverage and grade, geographic area of residence, school category, and social deprivation. Students residing in the most socially deprived areas (Q4 and Q5) had 32% (PAF = 5.3%) and 70% (PAF = 7.0%) higher odds, respectively, of being underimmunised compared to those residing in the least socially deprived areas. Students residing in socially deprived Q4 and Q5 neighbourhoods were enrolled in the majority (93%) of schools, those underimmunised were enrolled in 82% of schools, and 38 schools (11.8%) enrolled 10 or more underimmunised students. Based on these results, the baseline program was strengthened in all schools, and 38 schools were prioritised to receive enhanced public health interventions. CONCLUSIONS: This study confirmed previously reported associations, namely the relationship between social deprivation and underimmunisation, and underscores the need for targeted outreach to socially vulnerable families within the context of a publicly funded school immunisation program.

title: What is the best frequency to suppress 3D real stimuli from consciousness? A CFS study
abstract_text: This study will replicate a work by Zhu and colleagues on pictorial stimuli (2016), to investigate the appropriate frequency at which CFS can suppress 3D stimuli. In CFS, we usually present rapidly flashing patterns to the dominant eye, meanwhile the other one looks at a stationary stimulus. This procedure leads to a suppression of the visibility of the unchanging stimulus (e.g., Yang et al., 2014; Sperandio et al., 2018). In this study, the participants will be exposed to a CFS pattern that will change, in turn, at 10 different frequencies (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 20, and 32 Hz). The participants will be instructed to press a button as quickly as possible when they saw a stimulus. In this way, we can calculate the average timing needed for a stimulus to arise into consciousness and find the frequency that elicits the greatest suppression. Typically, this study would involve the use of bCFS, with a reduction in the stimulus transparency and a resulting increase of contrast between the stimulus and the background. In this case, since we couldn't change the properties of the 3D real stimuli, we will wait for the stimulus to emerge into consciousness naturally and choose the manipulation that will provide us with the best suppression. This information could give us important information about the temporal limits of other experiment trials that can be really considered unconscious. Overstepping this temporal window will signal the timing where the participants, on average, are able to perceive the stimuli even in the unconscious condition (i.e., with CFS). This objective index of trial validity could be useful in a context where the subjective report (Perceptual Awareness Scale, see below) could be sometimes inaccurate or uncertain. We will also investigate if there are differences in presenting the CFS to the right or left eye, with regard to the supression time.
